title: The History of 7UP — The Drink Without a Single Owner
fullText: CocaCola has Sprite. Pepsi now has a rival in Dr. Pepper. And SevenUp has two owners at the same time. And that's not a metaphor. If you buy a Seven Up in the United States, your money goes to Curig Dr. Pepper. Yes, the same company I recently covered. But buy that exact same SevenUp almost anywhere else in the world. And the money goes to PepsiCo, Dr. Pepper's biggest competitor. One drink, one label. But behind the counter in New York and behind the counter in London are two bitter rivals who technically control the same brand. And that isn't even the strangest part of 7Up's history. The formula that became 7Up originally contained a psychiatric drug, a substance that was later used to treat bipolar disorder. It was added to the drink specifically because it was believed to improve people's moods. And the beverage was marketed almost like an anti-depressant in a bottle. 7Up entered the market just 2 weeks before the stock market crash of 1929, meaning Americans were being offered a drink advertised as a remedy for a bad mood just as the country was about to enter the Great Depression. And there's one more problem with this drink. The official story behind its name, the version repeated by virtually every article on the subject, including probably half the sources you would find yourself, may simply be wrong. I'll tell you how a soft drink containing a psychoactive drug survived the prohibition of its own key ingredient became the property of a tobacco company and eventually ended up split between two rival corporations and why the origin story that has been repeated for almost a century may be at least in part a complete invention. Charles Liper Grigg was born in 1868 in rural Missouri and eventually moved to St. Louis where he began working in advertising and sales for companies that bottled soft drinks. In 1920, he created an orange drink called Howdy and founded his own company to sell it. The problem was that America's orange soda market was already locked up. Orange Crush dominated the category and no matter how much effort Grigg put into Howdy, it continued losing ground year after year to the much stronger competitor. This was actually Grigg's second attempt to break into the orange soda business. Earlier, while working for another company, he had created a similar drink called Whistle, and the story had played out almost exactly the same way. Orange Crush simply left very little room for competitors. Instead of fighting for the same orange soda shelf space for a third time, Grigg decided to abandon the category altogether. For 2 years, he experimented with lemon lime formulas, a category where almost every small bottler at the time had its own version, but nobody had managed to build a truly national brand. In October 1929, Grigg finally released the result of those experiments onto the American market. Here was Grigg's real innovation and why the story of his drink goes far beyond simply creating a successful flavor. He added lithium citrate to the formula, a compound that was already being used in psychiatry to treat manic states and what we would now call bipolar disorder. Grigg was betting on a popular belief of the time that lithium could stabilize a person's mood and make them feel happier. And he didn't exactly hide the ingredient. He put it right in the product's original name, bib label lithiated lemon lime soda. The advertising promised exactly what you might expect from a drink built around that idea, a better mood. And the timing could hardly have been more ironic or more commercially convenient. The drink reached the market just two weeks before the stock market crash of 1929 and the beginning of the Great Depression. The following decade would bring poverty, anxiety, unemployment, and breadlines across America. And sitting on store shelves was a lemon lime soda that openly promised to make people feel better. One of its early advertising lines said it all. Take the ouch out of grouch. It's important to understand the context of the era. In the late 1920s, lithium was hardly considered dangerous or fringe. It had been prescribed for manic conditions since the 19th century. And by the 1930s, it was freely sold in dozens of patented health tonics without any special prescription. roughly the way vitamin supplements are sold today. Grigg didn't invent some radical new use for the substance. He simply became one of the first to put a fashionable ingredient directly into a mass market soft drink name instead of hiding it in the fine print of an ingredient list. Lithium remained in the formula for more than 20 years. Then in 1948, cases of lithium chloride poisoning began increasing in the United States. At the time, lithium chloride was being sold without meaningful oversight as a salt substitute for people with high blood pressure, and several of those cases ended in death. Regulators responded by taking a broader look at the use of lithium in consumer products. By 1950, the ingredient had been removed from the soda's formula for good. Today, lithium remains one of the principal medications used to treat bipolar disorder. Only now, it is strictly prescription only and carefully dosed by a physician rather than being poured by the gallon into a family soft drink. And this is where the story takes an unexpected turn. One that almost never appears in the official versions. Virtually every article about 7Up, including probably half of what you'll find online, repeats the same detail. The drink was originally called Bib Label Lithiated Lemon Lime Soda, and only later was it shortened to Seven Up. It's a beautiful story about a long, awkward name evolving into a concise brand. And it has been repeated even by serious publications, appearing in encyclopedic articles and reports from major news organizations, each time almost word for word. The problem is that judging by archival documents from the US patent and trademark office, the reality appears to have been exactly the opposite. Grigg filed a trademark application for 7Up as early as October 1928, a full year before the drink's official launch, stating that he had been using the name since August of that same year. There are no trademark applications for the name Bib Label Lithiated Lemon Lime Soda in the archives at all, neither from Grig nor from anyone else. Apparently, this was never the official name of the brand, but simply a description of the formula printed on a temporary label for test batches, something that someone eventually mistook for the actual name of the product. And ever since, that version has simply been copied from one article to another for nearly a century, accumulating increasingly confident details along the way, even though not a single archival document has ever confirmed it. As for the origin of the number seven, nobody knows the answer, and apparently nobody ever will. Grigg died in 1940 without ever publicly explaining where the name came from. Decades later, a company spokesperson could only shrug when journalists asked, "It's a mystery." There are dozens of theories from seven original ingredients to 7 ounces in the original bottle. There's even a theory involving playing cards and the number of points, but the company has never officially confirmed any of them, and Grigg took the answer to his grave. By the 1960s, 7Up was still a niche product compared with the enormous Coca-Cola and Pepsi brands. In 1967, the advertising agency JW Thompson proposed a move that would completely change the brand's strategy. Instead of competing directly with cola, 7Up would define itself as its complete opposite. That was the birth of the uncola. In the commercials, CocaCola style glasses were deliberately turned upside down as if the entire idea of cola had literally been flipped on its head. The ads were shot in a psychedelic, almost surreal aesthetic with bright colors and abstract shapes that made the brand visually stand out against the much more conservative advertising of its competitors. The face of the campaign was Trinidadian actor and dancer Jeffrey Holder. And by the standards of late 1960s American advertising, the choice itself was almost revolutionary. Holder became one of the first black actors to serve as the central face of a major national advertising campaign rather than appearing as a secondary character in the background. Before Uncola, the brand already had its own mascot, a cheerful character named Freshy Freddy, who appeared in the 1950s and promoted the drink in a much more traditional familyfriendly way. Once Uncola arrived, that image was abandoned almost immediately. The new audience of the 1960s was looking for rebellion, not a friendly neighbor from a poster, and the company decided not to cling to an old asset simply because it had once worked. The campaign fit perfectly with the spirit of the era. The counterculture of the 1960s was looking for ways to define itself against everything traditional and adult, while Cola had by then become firmly associated with the establishment. Within months, 7Up's market share grew by 30%. And by the mid 1970s, the drink had become the third largest soft drink brand in the world behind the two cola giants it had spent all those years deliberately defining itself against. Interestingly, Uncola didn't stop with advertising and even found its way into a world far removed from commercials. During the 1970s and 80s, SevenUp became almost a staple of home cooking. Far removed from its usual image as a soft drink. People poured it into gelatin desserts, added it to casserles with carrots and broccoli to mellow the flavor. And after prohibition ended, it became a classic mixer for the Seven and Seven cocktail, a combination of SevenUp and Seager Seven Crown Whiskey. With the name deliberately echoing the soft drink itself, very few soft drink brands can claim to have become part of not only advertising culture, but culinary culture as well. In 1978, the brand's founder's son died, and just a few months later, the 7Up company was hit by an aggressive takeover. The buyer was Philip Morris, the world's largest cigarette manufacturer, which paid roughly $520 million for a company whose entire advertising strategy had been built around the ideas of cleanliness and naturalenness. The irony only deepened four years later when the new owners launched one of the most successful campaigns in the brand's history. No caffeine. The message was printed directly on the label and repeated in virtually every commercial emphasizing that 7Up contained no caffeine unlike all of its major competitors. The campaign tapped into growing public concern about caffeine in soft drinks and triggered a surge in sales. It also forced the entire soft drink industry to take a fresh look at how it labeled and marketed its products. The result was a rather bizarre picture. A company making most of its money from the nicotine addiction of millions of smokers spent a decade running a brand whose central advertising claim was built around the fact that its product contained nothing addictive. Personally, I think this is one of the most underrated details in the entire corporate history of soft drinks. Such an obvious contradiction is rarely found inside a single press release. and Philip Morris itself clearly understood the value of diversification. Alongside SevenUp, the company was also acquiring Miller Brewing Company and food giant General Foods during those same years, apparently trying to reduce the corporation's dependence on tobacco revenue in case regulators eventually tightened the rules around cigarettes, which of course is exactly what happened. By the mid 1980s, Philip Morris decided that tobacco was a more attractive business than soft drinks and began selling SevenUp off in pieces. And that decision would determine the brand's fate for the next 40 years. In 1986, the international rights to 7Up were sold to PepsiCo for $246 million, meaning the brand ended up in the hands of the very historical rival it had spent decades attacking through its Uncola advertising. The American business was sold separately to the investment group Hicks and Hos, which merged it with Dr. Pepper in 1988, creating Dr. Pepper 7Up. Since then, the American side of the brand has changed hands several more times. Cadbury Schweps in 1995, then Dr. Pepper Smapple, and finally the 2018 merger with Curig created today's Curig Dr. Pepper. The international side, meanwhile, stayed quietly with PepsiCo for all 40 years and never went anywhere. Neither side ever tried to buy out the other and reunite the brand under one roof. Perhaps because exclusive regional rights were more valuable to both companies than owning the entire brand. Or perhaps because after four decades, the question of who actually owns 7Up simply stopped mattering to everyone except particularly persistent journalists. In practice, this creates some genuinely strange everyday situations. An American tourist visiting, say, London or Dubai can buy a can of Seven Up without realizing that the money is going to a company they normally think of as one of Coca-Cola's biggest rivals back home, even though Coca-Cola itself has absolutely nothing to do with 7Up in either market. And someone from almost anywhere else in the world who moves to the United States can discover that the SevenUp they grew up drinking is now produced by a completely different company, the same one that makes Dr. Pepper. The can looks almost exactly the same, but the money from that purchase goes to the opposite corporate camp. While Sprite spent decades strengthening its position inside Coca-Cola's enormous distribution network, 7Up found itself in a much less advantageous position. Within the Dr. Pepper Snapple portfolio, it was always a secondary brand, receiving less advertising support than the company's flagship namesake. In the 1990s, the company even tried changing its formula to compete directly with Sprite, but the move produced no significant breakthrough. By the end of the decade, the company tried to recover some of 7Up's cultural relevance with the provocative Make SevenUp Yours campaign featuring comedian Orlando Jones. The ads relied on double entandras and humor that was unusually bold for the time, generating considerable public reaction, including complaints from parent organizations about the sexual undertones of a brand that had spent decades presenting itself as familyfriendly. At the same time, television screens introduced a silent mascot named Spot, an animated red dot taken from the brand's logo, expressing emotions through squeaks and gestures alongside the similarly styled Phtood Daido character used in international markets. Interestingly, even the brand's logo has changed far less over the past century than its ownership. The recognizable seven with the red dot in various forms has accompanied the drink since the middle of the 20th century, surviving a tobacco company, three different corporate owners, and the complete division of the brand between two separate companies. And yet the packaging on a store shelf in New York and one in London looks remarkably similar today, despite the fact that two completely different companies are responsible for producing and selling it. In the 1990s, the red dot from the logo even developed a video game career of its own. The platformer Cool Spot, released for consoles and computers, featured the character Spot, rescuing smaller Spot branded bottles scattered throughout the levels from a villain. The game was successful enough for critics to consider it one of the better advertising game tie-ins of the 1990s. A rare case where a marketing product for a soft drink was praised as a legitimate video game in its own right rather than dismissed as nothing more than a promotional stunt. Today, 7Up consistently trails Sprite in the lemon lime soda market in most places around the world. Part of that can be attributed to less aggressive marketing and part to the simple consequences of split ownership. When the same brand belongs to two different corporations with different priorities in different parts of the world, it becomes difficult to build a unified global strategy that can operate as consistently as Coca-Cola has done with Sprite for decades. There is also an amusing connection to my two previous stories. While Dr. Pepper spent years steadily overtaking Pepsi in the United States through seasonal limited edition flavors. That same Dr. Pepper Snapple portfolio spent decades underinvesting in its own lemon lime asset, 7Up, allowing Coca-Cola Sprite to pull comfortably ahead on that separate front. The same corporate portfolio was effectively winning its war against Pepsi in one product category while losing its battle against Coca-Cola in another simply because resources and management attention are finite even inside a multi-billion dollar corporation. At the same time, PepsiCo itself ended up in an almost mirror image situation. The company that already has its own lemon lime drink, Merinda, in parts of its portfolio and competes directly with Sprite around the world also controls the international rights to 7Up, the historic rival of the cola giants. In other words, the brand that built its identity around standing against Pepsi is now in roughly half the world literally working for Pepsi, simply in a different part of the planet where hardly anyone seems to find the contradiction particularly strange. Let's return to where we started. Two rival soft drink giants that technically co-own the same brand simply in different parts of the world. A drink that began as a psychiatric drug in a bottle, promising to lift the spirits of an entire country just before the greatest economic collapse of the 20th century went on to survive the banning of its own signature ingredient, a decade under the control of a cigarette company selling it as an emblem of purity, and finally a permanent split between two corporations that in almost every other situation do nothing but compete with each other. And the story of how the drink got its name, repeated for nearly a century, turns out when the archives are examined closely, to be most likely nothing more than a beautiful legend that nobody ever bothered to verify. When you compare Seven Up with the stories of Pepsi, Sprite, Dr. Pepper, and Red Bull, the difference becomes immediately obvious. Despite all their twists and turns, those brands remained intact. Each had one company making the decisions, one recipe, and one overall strategy. 7Up is the only brand in this group that is literally divided between two competing corporations and has continued to exist in that split state for nearly 40 decades. Perhaps that is why it never managed to become the dominant leader in its category. It is difficult to be anyone's top priority when you have two owners at the same time, each with dozens of other brands that matter more. If you enjoyed this story, subscribe. There's more coming. And here's the question for the comments. What surprised you more? The lithium and the soda or the fact that 7Up is technically owned by both Pepsi and Pepsi's rival at the same time? Personally, the hardest part for me to write was the story behind the name. It's frustrating to discover that a story repeated for almost a century was probably nothing more than someone's mistake, copied by dozens of writers until it eventually became an established Act.
fullTextVi: CocaCola có Sprite. Pepsi giờ đã có đối thủ Dr. Hạt tiêu. Và SevenUp có hai chủ sở hữu cùng một lúc. Và đó không phải là một phép ẩn dụ. Nếu bạn mua Seven Up ở Hoa Kỳ, tiền của bạn sẽ chuyển đến Tiến sĩ Curig Hạt tiêu. Vâng, chính là công ty mà tôi mới bảo hiểm. Nhưng hãy mua chính xác SevenUp đó ở hầu hết mọi nơi trên thế giới. Và tiền sẽ thuộc về PepsiCo, Tiến sĩ Đối thủ cạnh tranh lớn nhất của Pepper. Một đồ uống, một nhãn hiệu. Nhưng đằng sau quầy hàng ở New York và đằng sau quầy hàng ở London là hai đối thủ gay gắt kiểm soát cùng một thương hiệu về mặt kỹ thuật. Và đó thậm chí không phải là phần kỳ lạ nhất trong lịch sử của 7Up. Công thức trở thành 7Up ban đầu có chứa một loại thuốc tâm thần, một chất có tên là sau này được sử dụng để điều trị rối loạn lưỡng cực. Nó được thêm vào đồ uống đặc biệt vì nó được cho là có tác dụng cải thiện tâm trạng. Và đồ uống này được bán trên thị trường gần giống như thuốc chống trầm cảm đóng trong chai. 7Up gia nhập thị trường chỉ 2 tuần trước khi thị trường chứng khoán sụp đổ năm 1929, có nghĩa là người Mỹ được mời uống một loại đồ uống được quảng cáo là phương thuốc chữa bệnh tồi tệ đúng lúc đất nước sắp bước vào cuộc Đại suy thoái. Và còn một vấn đề nữa với thức uống này. Câu chuyện chính thức đằng sau cái tên của nó, phiên bản được lặp lại trong hầu hết mọi bài viết trên chủ đề, có lẽ bao gồm một nửa số nguồn mà bạn tự tìm thấy, có thể chỉ đơn giản là sai. Tôi sẽ kể cho bạn nghe làm thế nào một loại nước giải khát có chứa thuốc kích thích thần kinh vẫn sống sót sau lệnh cấm thành phần chính của nó đã trở thành tài sản của một công ty thuốc lá và cuối cùng cuối cùng đã bị chia rẽ giữa hai tập đoàn đối thủ và tại sao câu chuyện nguồn gốc lại có được lặp đi lặp lại trong gần một thế kỷ có thể ít nhất một phần là một hoàn chỉnh sự phát minh. Charles Liper Grigg sinh năm 1868 ở vùng nông thôn Missouri và cuối cùng chuyển đến St. Louis nơi anh bắt đầu làm việc trong lĩnh vực quảng cáo và bán hàng cho các công ty đóng chai nước mềm đồ uống. Năm 1920, ông tạo ra một loại đồ uống màu cam có tên Howdy và thành lập công ty riêng để bán nó. Vấn đề là thị trường soda cam của Mỹ đã bị đóng cửa. Orange Crush thống trị hạng mục này và bất kể Grigg đã nỗ lực bao nhiêu Xin chào, nó tiếp tục mất vị thế từ năm này qua năm khác vào tay đối thủ cạnh tranh mạnh hơn nhiều. Đây thực sự là nỗ lực thứ hai của Grigg để thâm nhập vào lĩnh vực kinh doanh nước ngọt cam. Trước đó, khi làm việc cho một công ty khác, anh đã tạo ra một loại đồ uống tương tự có tên Whistle, và câu chuyện đã diễn ra gần như giống hệt như vậy. Orange Crush đơn giản là để lại rất ít chỗ cho các đối thủ cạnh tranh. Thay vì tranh giành cùng một không gian kệ soda màu cam lần thứ ba, Grigg quyết định từ bỏ hoàn toàn hạng mục này. Trong 2 năm, anh ấy đã thử nghiệm các công thức chanh chanh, một danh mục mà hầu hết mọi nhà đóng chai nhỏ vào thời điểm đó có phiên bản riêng, nhưng chưa ai có được xây dựng một thương hiệu quốc gia đích thực. Vào tháng 10 năm 1929, Grigg cuối cùng đã công bố kết quả của những thí nghiệm đó trên của Mỹ. chợ. Đây là sự đổi mới thực sự của Grigg và tại sao câu chuyện về đồ uống của anh ấy lại lan xa không chỉ đơn giản là tạo ra một hương vị thành công. Ông đã thêm lithium citrate vào công thức, một hợp chất đã được sử dụng trong tâm thần học để điều trị các trạng thái hưng cảm và cái mà ngày nay chúng ta gọi là rối loạn lưỡng cực. Grigg đang đặt cược vào niềm tin phổ biến thời bấy giờ rằng lithium có thể ổn định tâm trạng của một người và làm cho họ cảm thấy hạnh phúc hơn. Và anh ấy không hề giấu chính xác thành phần. Anh đặt ngay vào tên gốc của sản phẩm, nhãn yếm chanh dây soda. Quảng cáo hứa hẹn chính xác những gì bạn có thể mong đợi từ một loại đồ uống được xây dựng xung quanh đó ý tưởng, một tâm trạng tốt hơn. Và thời điểm khó có thể mỉa mai hơn hoặc thuận tiện hơn về mặt thương mại. Đồ uống này được tung ra thị trường chỉ hai tuần trước khi thị trường chứng khoán sụp đổ 1929 và sự khởi đầu của cuộc Đại suy thoái. Thập kỷ tiếp theo sẽ mang đến nghèo đói, lo lắng, thất nghiệp và thiếu lương thực trên khắp nước Mỹ. Và nằm trên kệ của cửa hàng là một loại soda chanh được hứa hẹn công khai làm cho mọi người cảm thấy tốt hơn. Một trong những dòng quảng cáo đầu tiên của nó đã nói lên tất cả. Hãy thoát khỏi sự cáu kỉnh. Điều quan trọng là phải hiểu bối cảnh của thời đại. Vào cuối những năm 1920, lithium hầu như không được coi là nguy hiểm hay đáng lo ngại. Nó đã được kê đơn cho các tình trạng hưng cảm từ thế kỷ 19. Và đến những năm 1930, nó được bán tự do dưới dạng hàng chục loại thuốc bổ sức khỏe đã được cấp bằng sáng chế mà không cần bất kỳ đơn thuốc đặc biệt nào. đại khái là cách bán thuốc bổ sung vitamin ngày nay. Grigg đã không phát minh ra một số cách sử dụng hoàn toàn mới cho chất này. Đơn giản là anh ấy đã trở thành một trong những người đầu tiên đưa nguyên liệu thời trang trực tiếp vào một tên nước giải khát dành cho thị trường đại chúng thay vì giấu nó trong bản in đẹp của một danh sách thành phần. Lithium vẫn còn trong công thức trong hơn 20 năm. Sau đó vào năm 1948, các trường hợp ngộ độc lithium clorua bắt đầu gia tăng ở Hoa Kỳ. Vào thời điểm đó, lithium clorua đang được bán mà không có sự giám sát đáng kể dưới dạng muối thay thế cho những người bị huyết áp cao, và một số trường hợp trong số đó đã kết thúc bằng cái chết. Các cơ quan quản lý phản ứng bằng cách xem xét rộng hơn việc sử dụng lithium trong người tiêu dùng các sản phẩm. Đến năm 1950, thành phần này đã bị loại bỏ vĩnh viễn khỏi công thức soda. Ngày nay, lithium vẫn là một trong những loại thuốc chính được sử dụng để điều trị rối loạn lưỡng cực. Chỉ có điều bây giờ nó chỉ được kê đơn nghiêm ngặt và được bác sĩ kê đơn cẩn thận hơn hơn là đổ từng gallon vào nước ngọt của gia đình. Và đây chính là lúc câu chuyện rẽ sang một hướng bất ngờ. Một thứ gần như không bao giờ xuất hiện trong các phiên bản chính thức. Hầu như mọi bài viết về 7Up, bao gồm cả một nửa những gì bạn tìm thấy trên mạng, đều lặp lại cùng một chi tiết. Thức uống này ban đầu có tên là Bib Label Lithied Lemon Lime Soda, và sau này mới có tên nó đã được rút ngắn thành Seven Up. Đó là một câu chuyện hay về một cái tên dài và vụng về phát triển thành một thương hiệu ngắn gọn.
